Question 1: Choosing an SVM kernel

Use saheart.csv from the combined ZIP. As in Homework 7, predict chd using the same nine predictors, coding famhist as 1 for Absent and 2 for Present.

Compare SVMs with a linear kernel, polynomial kernels of degrees 2 (quadratic), 3, and 4, and a radial basis kernel. Choose no more than 20 candidate settings in total across these kernels. Vary the cost CC for each kernel and the radial scale γ\gamma for the radial kernel. State any other kernel settings you hold fixed.

The response is chd and the predictors are the other nine variables, with famhist coded 1 for Absent and 2 for Present. The observations are split at random into five folds (seed 432), and the same folds are used for every candidate. In each fold, the predictors are centered and scaled using only the fitting observations, and the same centers and scales are applied to the validation observations. Held fixed for all kernels: the polynomial kernel is (gamma times the inner product plus 1) raised to the degree, with gamma = 1/9 and the constant term equal to 1; no class weights; the default stopping tolerance. The cross-validation error of a candidate is the mean misclassification rate over the five folds.

Divide the observations into five folds yourself and use the same folds for all candidates. Standardize predictors using only the fitting observations in each fold. Report the candidate settings and their mean cross-validation misclassification rates. Which kernel and settings do you prefer? Give a brief justification.

library(e1071)
heart <- read.csv("data/saheart.csv")
heart$famhist <- match(heart$famhist, c("Absent", "Present"))
y <- factor(heart$chd, levels = c(0, 1))
X <- as.matrix(heart[, setdiff(names(heart), "chd")])
n <- nrow(X)

set.seed(432)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n))

radial <- expand.grid(cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = c(0.01, 0.1))
radial$kernel <- "radial"
radial$degree <- NA
cand <- rbind(
  data.frame(kernel = "linear", degree = NA, cost = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10), gamma = NA),
  data.frame(kernel = "polynomial", degree = 2, cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = NA),
  data.frame(kernel = "polynomial", degree = 3, cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = NA),
  data.frame(kernel = "polynomial", degree = 4, cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = NA),
  radial[, c("kernel", "degree", "cost", "gamma")]
)
nrow(cand)
[1] 19
cv_err <- numeric(nrow(cand))
for (j in seq_len(nrow(cand))) {
  errs <- numeric(5)
  for (k in 1:5) {
    tr <- folds != k
    mu <- colMeans(X[tr, ])
    s <- apply(X[tr, ], 2, sd)
    Xtr <- scale(X[tr, ], center = mu, scale = s)
    Xva <- scale(X[!tr, ], center = mu, scale = s)
    g <- if (cand$kernel[j] == "radial") cand$gamma[j] else 1 / ncol(X)
    deg <- if (is.na(cand$degree[j])) 3 else cand$degree[j]
    fit <- svm(x = Xtr, y = y[tr], type = "C-classification",
               kernel = cand$kernel[j], degree = deg, cost = cand$cost[j],
               gamma = g, coef0 = 1, scale = FALSE)
    pred <- predict(fit, Xva)
    errs[k] <- mean(pred != y[!tr])
  }
  cv_err[j] <- mean(errs)
}
cand$kernel_label <- ifelse(cand$kernel == "polynomial",
                            paste0("polynomial, degree ", cand$degree), cand$kernel)
res <- data.frame(Kernel = cand$kernel_label, C = cand$cost,
                  Gamma = cand$gamma, CV_error = round(cv_err, 4))
knitr::kable(res, row.names = FALSE)
Kernel C Gamma CV_error
linear 0.01 NA 0.2770
linear 0.10 NA 0.2791
linear 1.00 NA 0.2813
linear 10.00 NA 0.2813
polynomial, degree 2 0.10 NA 0.2706
polynomial, degree 2 1.00 NA 0.2793
polynomial, degree 2 10.00 NA 0.2944
polynomial, degree 3 0.10 NA 0.2749
polynomial, degree 3 1.00 NA 0.3183
polynomial, degree 3 10.00 NA 0.3160
polynomial, degree 4 0.10 NA 0.2814
polynomial, degree 4 1.00 NA 0.3399
polynomial, degree 4 10.00 NA 0.3594

radial 10.00 0.01 0.2684

best <- res[order(res$CV_error), ]
knitr::kable(head(best, 5), row.names = FALSE)
Kernel C Gamma CV_error
radial 1.00 0.01 0.2619
radial 10.00 0.01 0.2684
polynomial, degree 2 0.10 NA 0.2706
polynomial, degree 3 0.10 NA 0.2749
linear 0.01 NA 0.2770

I prefer the radial kernel with C = 1 and gamma = 0.01. It has the lowest mean five-fold cross-validation misclassification rate, 0.2619, which means about 26.2 percent of observations were misclassified in validation.

The linear kernel (0.2770 to 0.2813 across the four costs), the quadratic polynomial with C = 0.1 (0.2706), and the cubic polynomial with C = 0.1 (0.2749) are all close. The best candidates lie within about 1.5 percentage points of each other. With 462 observations, the sampling uncertainty of an error rate near 0.26 is about 2 percentage points, so I would not claim that the radial kernel is clearly better than the linear or quadratic kernels.

Two patterns are clear. First, more flexible settings do worse: the polynomial error rises with the degree and with the cost (for example, degree 4 with C = 10 gives 0.3594), which suggests overfitting. Second, the radial kernel is sensitive to its settings. Radial with C = 0.1 and gamma = 0.01 or 0.1 gives about 0.345, close to 0.3463, the proportion of observations with chd = 1 (160 of 462). That is what we would expect from a model that is too heavily regularized and predicts almost everyone as no heart disease. With gamma = 0.1 and C = 10, the error rises to 0.3399, again showing overfitting.

I choose the radial setting because it has the lowest cross-validation error, but because the linear and quadratic kernels are nearly as good and simpler, either would be a reasonable choice. Limitations: the best gamma, 0.01, is the smallest value in my grid, so a smaller value might do as well or better, and choosing the minimum of 19 cross-validation errors makes the winning error slightly optimistic. I did not use a separate test set for this question.

Question 2: Write and use a short SVM analysis skill

In Homework 8, you reviewed another student’s skill. Review the comments and suggestions you received on your own Homework 7 skill. Use what you learned from both sides of the peer review to write a new, shorter skill for SVM model fitting.

Write the skill by hand. Create a SKILL.md with a short name and description in YAML frontmatter. Write the entire file yourself, without asking AI to draft or edit it. The instruction body after the closing --- of the frontmatter must be no more than 50 lines, including blank lines. Keep the skill independent of any particular dataset, variable names, or observed results, and load it only when you explicitly invoke it.

Your skill should direct the agent to:

  1. judge whether the data are suitable for an SVM analysis;
  2. choose which kernels to consider and explain why;
  3. identify tuning parameters and a method for tuning them;
  4. choose an evaluation method that supports selecting a final model;
  5. require a compact figure and table that justify the choices;
  6. interpret the fit and report the key numerical results; and
  7. prioritize the evidence needed to justify the final model in no more than one printed page at 11-point font.

Apply the skill. Explicitly invoke your skill to analyze saheart.csv, using the same response, nine predictors, and famhist coding as in Question 1. Provide these data details when invoking the skill, not in the skill itself. Let the skill guide the analysis, then check the resulting report and calculations.

Submit the results. Include the one-page, 11-point analysis report in your Homework 09 submission and append the complete contents of your SKILL.md afterward. The appended skill is outside the one-page limit.

My one-page report is in ‘report-page.png’.

The skill is in the code block below.

---
name: svm-model-fitting
description: Fit, tune, evaluate, and report support vector machine classification models. Apply only when explicitly invoked.
---

# Scope
Use only when explicitly invoked. Include the dataset, response, predictors, and other relevant information or intructions. Keep the workflow datatset-independent.

# Analysis workflow
1. Check the sample size, response classes, missing or nonfinite values, duplicate values, predictor types, class imbalance, data leakage, and group/time dependence. Explain any limitations before fitting.
2. Split the data into a stratified training and test set, respecting group/time structure. Set the seed to 90210. Do not use the test set until model selection is complete.
3. Standardize numeric predictors using training-fold statistics only. Encode categorical predictors appropriately. Fit all preprocessing separately inside each cross-validation fold.
4. Compare a linear kernel, which fits a straight boundary, with an RBF kernel, which allows nonlinear boundaries. Include a polynomial kernel only when justified by plausible interactions or curvature and adequate sample size. Explain any and all exclusions.
5. Tune cost C for every kernel; tune gamma for RBF and polynomial kernels and degree for polynomial kernels. Use a compact, documented grid and stratified training-only cross-validation. Reuse identical folds across candidates.
6. Select by pooled out-of-fold classification error unless class imbalance or unequal error costs justify a metric such as balanced accuracy or ROC AUC. Report the metric and rationale. Use cross-validation uncertainty to contextualize small differences.
7. Record convergence warnings, failed fits, selected parameters, class-specific performance, and confusion matrices. Do not silently discard failed folds or tune using test results.
8. Refit the selected pipeline on all training data, then evaluate it once on the untouched test set. Report test mistakes/total and error rate, plus a relevant secondary metric. If the test set is compromised or unavailable, state this clearly and do not invent a test result.

# Report

Produce a professional PDF of no more than one printed page at 11-point font. Prioritize evidence for model suitability, kernel choice, tuning, evaluation, and final selection.
Include a compact table of candidate kernels, selected tuning parameters, cross-validation errors, and uncertainty; label failures explicitly.
Include a legible comparison figure with uncertainty bars for cross-validation errors, using the same metric as the table.
State the selected model, test results, interpretation, limitations, and a brief conclusion. Explain whether the performance difference is meaningful given uncertainty.
Verify calculations, figure labels, page count, and readability before declaring completion. If any requirement cannot be met, identify it explicitly rather than claiming full compliance.
